data: European Space Agency (Huygens probe, carried to Saturn by NASA/ASI Cassini orbiter)

318 kg ESA entry probe — aeroshell, 3 parachutes, 6 science packages (HASI, GCMS, DISR, ACP, SSP, DWE). Designed to survive 2.5-hour atmospheric descent through Titan's nitrogen–methane atmosphere to the surface.
~6 km/s (entry deceleration from 6 km/s hypersonic to surface)

© ESA / NASA / JPL-Caltech / University of Arizona — Huygens probe data public domain. The Huygens probe rode aboard NASA's Cassini spacecraft on the 7-year VVEJGA interplanetary cruise to the Saturn system. Released 2004-12-25, it coasted 20 days before entering Titan's atmosphere on 2005-01-14. A heat shield slowed it from 6 km/s to subsonic, then three parachute stages (main chute at 160 km, drogue at 120 km, stabiliser for the final descent) let it drift for 2 hours 27 minutes through the haze, transmitting 350 images and full atmospheric profiles before touching down on a floodplain of rounded water-ice pebbles and a thin veneer of liquid methane. The landing site (10.3°S, 192.3°W) lies in a dark lowland drained by methane rivers from brighter highlands. Huygens returned data from the surface for ~72 minutes until Cassini set below its radio horizon. First and only soft landing in the outer solar system.

Titan IVB / Centaur lifts the 5712 kg Cassini–Huygens stack from Cape Canaveral. Huygens rides aboard Cassini as an attached entry probe; the 7-year VVEJGA cruise to Saturn begins.
First Venus flyby (1998-04-26, 284 km altitude). Gravity assist raises the spacecraft's aphelion as part of the energy-building VVEJGA sequence.
Second Venus flyby (1999-06-24, 623 km). Together with the first assist, sets up the Earth flyby 55 days later.
1171 km above the South Pacific (1999-08-18). The orbit is now energetic enough to cross Jupiter's.
9.85 million km from Jupiter (2000-12-30). Final assist delivers the remaining velocity for Saturn arrival.

Cassini's main-engine burn (2004-07-01) captures the stack into Saturn orbit. Huygens remains dormant, attached to Cassini, for the next six months while the orbiter homes in on a Titan flyby geometry.
Huygens released from Cassini on 2004-12-25, coasting toward Titan on a ballistic trajectory with no propulsion. The probe then hibernated for 20 days.

2005-01-14: entry at 6 km/s, heat shield slows to subsonic; main chute at 160 km deploys; 2.5-hour parachute descent through Titan's haze transmitting 350 images and full atmospheric profiles. Touchdown on a floodplain of rounded water-ice pebbles at 10.3°S, 192.3°W — the first and only soft landing in the outer solar system.
First and only soft landing in the outer solar system — parachuted through Titan's atmosphere on 2005-01-14

Huygens was sent not to orbit but to fall. Strapped to Cassini for seven years, it detached on Christmas Day 2004 and coasted alone toward Titan for twenty days. When it hit Titan's atmosphere at six kilometres per second, a heat shield bought the time it needed; then three parachute stages slowed it for two and a half hours through an orange haze no instrument had ever crossed. It photographed river valleys, measured wind speeds, smelled the atmosphere — and touched down on a floodplain of rounded water-ice pebbles. It was the first landing ever made in the outer solar system, and no spacecraft has landed there since.

ESA's Huygens probe rode aboard NASA's Cassini spacecraft on a 7-year interplanetary cruise to the Saturn system, arriving at Saturn in July 2004. Released on 2004-12-25, it coasted for 20 days before entering Titan's nitrogen–methane atmosphere on 2005-01-14 at 6 km/s. An aeroshell slowed the probe to subsonic speed; three successive parachute stages then guided it through 2 hours 27 minutes of descent, collecting the first direct measurements of Titan's atmosphere — temperature, pressure, wind, and chemical composition at all altitudes. The probe transmitted 350 images during descent and continued transmitting from the surface for 72 minutes, revealing a floodplain of rounded water-ice pebbles beneath a thin veneer of liquid methane at 10.3°S, 192.3°W.
Titan IVB / Centaur lifts the Cassini–Huygens stack. Huygens rides as an attached probe for the 7-year VVEJGA cruise.
Cassini (and attached Huygens) captured into Saturn orbit 2004-07-01.
Probe released from Cassini 2004-12-25; 20-day ballistic coast to Titan.
2005-01-14: heat shield, three parachute stages, 2.5-hour descent, surface landing — first outer-solar-system soft landing.
